27.s: Phillips says there was little to hear; they knew the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, and later the three of them played Bix and Trumbauer in three-part harmony.
27.q: Yeah, we used to listen to them, different things. Then after that, we got together, Lester, Pete and myself... We used to get together and play Bix, Frankie Trumbauer... We played together, played it three-part harmony.

27.t: Records they listened to in 1926: Armstrong, Henderson, Goldkette, Bix
27.s: Phillips lists Louis Armstrong's Hot Five, Fletcher Henderson, Jean Goldkette, Red Nichols, Trumbauer, Bix and Goodman as what everyone was hearing.
27.q: Well, that was the general kind of music that everybody listened to. Then the band that everybody listened to was Jean Goldkette.

27.t: Learning Bix and Trumbauer solos: Singing the Blues, Miss Clementine, Louisiana
27.s: Phillips lists records they learned, including Bix and Trumbauer solos on Miss Clementine with Goldkette and Louisiana with Whiteman.
27.q: : Yeah, let's see now. Red Nichols was out there a lot way before Bix -- I mean, real popular. He was probably more popular than Bix was for a long time -- Red Nichols and His Five Pennies.

27.t: Mississippi Mud and How Happy We Can Be: solos Lester learned
27.s: Phillips and Dupre sort out which Mississippi Mud record had Bix's break, and Phillips names How Happy We Can Be from Bix's small group.
27.q: : But I'm talking about the one that he made with Paul Whiteman... The Rhythm Boys sing "Mississippi Mud" with Whiteman.

27.t: Lester plays Singing the Blues; learning In A Mist in three-part harmony
27.s: Lester played Singing the Blues around the house; Phillips explains records seldom named players, and how Lester gave Phillips and Pete Jones harmony parts for Bix's In A Mist.
27.q: Yeah, Frankie... Yeah, there was about five or six of them. And I was listening to it, I said, "Man, who's that cat blowin' that trumpet?" -- like that, you know. He said, "His name is Bix." At that time, you had to know who it was, because they didn't put the names on the records. Very few records…

27.t: Hawkins, Stump Evans and Jimmy Dorsey on record
27.s: Phillips explains Hawkins was heard only in big-band solos while Trumbauer's small-group records showed more; Lester listened to Prince Robinson and not much to Dorsey.
27.q: : Hawkins didn't have too much out. See, the thing about Hawkins and them, Hawkins and them didn't play too much...only with the band. But see, Frankie and them made records with the small groups, where you could really dig 'em. See, you'd dig a cat when he's out there playing in the small group…

27.t: What Lester liked to hear in 1933: Teagarden's break on Dinah
27.s: Lester listened little but liked Jack Teagarden's riff on Red Nichols's Dinah; Phillips describes how Teagarden changed the trombone.
27.q: Yeah. He never did too much listening. He'd hear some things, and say "That sounds all right" -- you know, like that. But I mean, he...

106.t: Improvised Dixieland tunes and American records bought in Berlin
106.s: They improvised on standards like Tiger Rag; later in Berlin a music dealer held every new Red Nichols, Wolverines and Henderson release for him.
106.q: "Tiger Rag," and "Way Down Yonder in New Orleans," and things like that, you know. "I Wish I Could Shimmy Like My Sister Kate"

106.t: American jazz records reach Berlin and affect his style
106.s: Records by Nichols, the Wolverines, Trumbauer, Henderson and Ellington arrived; Briggs says they influenced but did not change his style, and he played around the melody for patrons.
106.q: Yes, yes. Recordings started coming over, and the orchestras started being pretty popular. And you had -- Red Nichols was already on the scene. The Wolverines were on the scene. Frankie Trumbauer came on the scene. And about the same time with Fletcher Henderson and the Duke was just beginning.

106.t: Paul Whiteman, Henry Busse and bandsmen buying records
106.s: He recalls Whiteman's records and a Berlin dealer's pride in Henry Busse; the band bought records like hot cakes, with Bix, Trumbauer and Miff Mole as influences.
106.q: That was before Paul Whiteman. That was entirely different. Then at about the same time, Paul Whiteman -- I heard Paul Whiteman's record, with Bussey the trumpet player.

172.t: Which bands the Tuxedo men copied from records
172.s: Ridgley says they learned from anyone with a popular record, including Dixieland bands and Paul Whiteman.
172.q: Everyone that had a good record. Everyone that had something that the people liked. That's how we went about it. And we would learn it.

40.t: His records and favorite trumpet players
40.s: He owns 30 or 40 LPs and blends Bunk Johnson, Bix and King Oliver. He likes Johnny Wiggs and thinks of Emmett Hardy, who Conner says never recorded.
40.q: Uh, I, I have, uh, I guess I have about 30 or 40 records of my own, you know. And, uh, I think most of the stuff I might have learned right off those records, you know, listening to the records and just pick it up.

572.t: Records he listened to as a young man
572.s: He owned King Oliver, Rhythm Kings and Wolverines records and admired Bix.
572.ch: Wider talk: bands, places and players
572.q: Well, the only, the only, the only, I had a collection of, uh, of all the good records of sports. My, my, my taste was good. Mm-hmm. I had all, all, all, all the, all the Rhythm King records and, and King Oliver records, and stuff like that, see. Mm-hmm. But then my kid brothers got into the…

641.t: Hearing the Bix records and race
641.s: Joe says they were told the Bix and Trumbauer records were by White musicians, and the new style took Black and White musicians by storm.
641.ch: Los Angeles with Mutt Carey and the taxi dances
641.q: We was wondering who it was... Because they had come up with such a distinct style! And today, though, those are nice records. Good arrangements, well-played to my idea. I just like them.

91.t: Trumbauer records and the Benson orchestra
91.s: Carter recalls hearing Trumbauer first with the Benson orchestra and then on Singin' the Blues.
91.q: Yes, Frankie Trombar, and I didn't -- I wasn't impressed by too much else of the orchestra with which he was playing. I remember he was playing with the Benson orchestra of Chicago, and the record that I did like of his that I think I even heard before I heard "Singin' The Blues" -- now…

418.t: Singin' the Blues, Trumbauer and Red Nichols
418.s: Trumbauer's Singin' the Blues solo was pretty and original; he also liked Red Nichols's bands, a different jazz from Fletcher Henderson's.
418.ch: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
418.q: No, the record was all right. It was great! Yeah, that band was great anyhow. I liked Frankie Trumbauer. I had seen Red Nichols' bands. I used to like them.

611.t: Listening to white groups: Red Nichols and Miff Mole
611.s: Asked what modern records he followed, Waters names the Goofus Five, the Clarence Williams Five and white groups such as Red Nichols and Miff Mole, who knocked him out with their musicianship.
611.q: Well, I just got through telling you about the Goofus Five and things like that and the Clarence Williams Five. Then I listened to groups, like the white groups like Red Nichols and Miff Mole and -

7.t: Idols Frankie Trumbauer and Red Nichols
7.s: The two recall Trumbauer's C-melody solo on 'Singin' the Blues' and Thomas's admiration for Red Nichols and his Five Pennies.
7.q: Frankie Trumbauer was half of the saxophone players in the country in that day. Everybody learned how to play that one solo of Frank Trumbauer.
